title: Global Regulation Tracker
summary: Where animal testing for cosmetics is prohibited, permitted, or conditionally restricted. Each entry links to the primary instrument. Statutory language is quoted rather than paraphrased wherever the distinction matters.

statusKey.prohibited: Testing and the marketing of animal-tested cosmetics are both prohibited.
statusKey.partial: A prohibition exists but carries material exemptions, transition periods, or conflicting obligations under other law.
statusKey.permitted: No general prohibition. Testing is neither required nor forbidden by cosmetics law.
statusKey.required: Animal testing is mandated for at least some product categories.

jurisdictions.name: European Union
jurisdictions.headline: The most complete cosmetics ban in force — and the clearest example of how chemicals law can cut across it.
jurisdictions.instrument: Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 on cosmetic products, Articles 18 and 20

timeline.event: Testing ban on finished cosmetic products takes effect.
Testing ban extends to cosmetic ingredients. Marketing ban applies for all endpoints except repeated-dose toxicity, reproductive toxicity, and toxicokinetics.
Marketing ban becomes complete: cosmetics relying on new animal data for any endpoint may not be placed on the EU market.

The ECHA Board of Appeal upholds testing requirements under REACH for substances used exclusively in cosmetics, where the concern is worker or environmental exposure (Symrise, cases A-009-2018 and A-010-2018).

The Commission responds to the European Citizens' Initiative ‘Save Cruelty-Free Cosmetics’, which gathered over 1.2 million validated signatures, committing to a roadmap for phasing out animal testing in chemical safety assessment.

caveats: The cosmetics ban governs cosmetics law. It does not override Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 (REACH), under which a substance may still be tested on animals to characterise risks to workers or the environment.

A product can therefore be lawfully sold as ‘not tested on animals’ under cosmetics law while an ingredient in it has been animal-tested under chemicals law. This is the single most important gap for a reader to understand.

jurisdictions.name: United Kingdom
jurisdictions.headline: A licensing ban since 1998, retained EU marketing rules — and the same chemicals-law tension as the EU.
jurisdictions.instrument: Retained Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009; Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act 1986; Home Office licensing policy

timeline.event: The Home Office ceases issuing licences for testing finished cosmetic products and their ingredients on animals.
The EU marketing ban applies in the UK as an EU Member State.
Regulation 1223/2009 is retained in UK law following the end of the transition period; the marketing ban continues to apply.

The Home Office confirms in correspondence and subsequent litigation that licences had been granted for animal testing of substances also used as cosmetic ingredients, where required under UK REACH for worker and environmental safety.

caveats: The 1998 policy is a licensing policy, not a statutory prohibition. Its scope has been re-interpreted, which is why the 2023 disclosure was possible.
As in the EU, UK REACH obligations sit outside cosmetics law and can require animal data for the same substances.

jurisdictions.name: China
jurisdictions.headline: Pre-market testing is now avoidable for many imported products — but only if specific conditions are met, and not for every category.
jurisdictions.instrument: Cosmetic Supervision and Administration Regulation (CSAR), State Council Order No. 727; NMPA implementing rules

timeline.event: Domestically manufactured ‘non-special use’ cosmetics become exempt from mandatory pre-market animal testing.

CSAR takes effect. Imported ‘general cosmetics’ may be exempted from pre-market animal testing where the manufacturer holds a GMP certificate issued by the competent authority in the producing country and submits a product safety assessment.

‘Special cosmetics’ — hair dyes, perms, freckle-removing and whitening products, sunscreens, anti-hair-loss products, and products making new efficacy claims — remain subject to animal testing requirements.

caveats: The exemption is conditional, not automatic. A brand that cannot obtain the required GMP certification, or that sells a special-cosmetic category, is still testing.
Products intended for infants and children, and products using ingredients still within their monitoring period, fall outside the exemption.
Regulators retain the power to conduct post-market testing, which may involve animals. A brand's presence in the Chinese market therefore does not by itself prove either compliance or non-compliance.

jurisdictions.name: United States — Federal
jurisdictions.headline: No federal prohibition. Animal testing is neither required nor banned for cosmetics.
jurisdictions.instrument: Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act; Modernization of Cosmetics Regulation Act of 2022 (MoCRA)

timeline.event: MoCRA expands FDA authority over cosmetics — facility registration, product listing, safety substantiation, adverse event reporting — but does not restrict animal testing.
The FDA Modernization Act 2.0 removes the statutory animal-testing requirement for new drug applications. It concerns drugs, not cosmetics; the two are frequently conflated in coverage.

caveats: The FDA has long stated that it does not specifically require animal testing for cosmetics, while holding manufacturers responsible for substantiating safety by whatever means they choose.
The Humane Cosmetics Act has been introduced in successive Congresses without being enacted. Federal movement has come from the states instead.

jurisdictions.name: United States — States
jurisdictions.headline: A patchwork of state sales bans covering a large share of the US consumer market.
jurisdictions.instrument: State cruelty-free cosmetics acts, typically prohibiting the sale of cosmetics developed using new animal testing after a stated date
caveats: These are sales bans, not testing bans. They restrict what may be sold in the state, which is what gives them national commercial effect.
Most carry exemptions where testing is required by a foreign regulator or by another domestic agency, and where the data predate the effective date.
State law changes frequently. Treat this list as a starting point and confirm against the state's own statute before relying on it.

jurisdictions.name: India
jurisdictions.headline: The first South Asian country to ban both testing and the import of animal-tested cosmetics.
jurisdictions.instrument: Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, Rules 148-C and 135-B

timeline.event: Rule 148-C prohibits the testing of cosmetics on animals within India.
Rule 135-B prohibits the import of cosmetics tested on animals.

jurisdictions.name: Israel
jurisdictions.headline: An import and marketing ban in force since 2013.
jurisdictions.instrument: Amendment to the Cruelty to Animals (Animal Experimentation) Law, 1994

timeline.event: Domestic testing of cosmetics on animals prohibited.
Import and marketing of cosmetics tested on animals prohibited.

jurisdictions.name: South Korea
jurisdictions.headline: A manufacturing and import ban with exemptions where no validated alternative exists.

timeline.event: Ban on the manufacture and import of cosmetics tested on animals takes effect.

caveats: Exemptions apply where testing is required by another country's law, where an ingredient's safety cannot be established by a validated alternative, and for public health research.

jurisdictions.name: Taiwan
jurisdictions.headline: A testing ban with a narrow statutory exemption.
jurisdictions.instrument: Cosmetic Hygiene and Safety Act, Article 5

timeline.event: Prohibition on animal testing for cosmetics takes effect.

caveats: Exemptions exist for special-purpose cosmetics and where testing is necessary to prove safety and no alternative is available.

jurisdictions.name: Australia
jurisdictions.headline: A ban on the use of new animal test data for chemicals introduced solely for cosmetic use.

timeline.event: Prohibition on using new animal test data to support the introduction of industrial chemicals used solely as cosmetic ingredients.

caveats: The prohibition attaches to the use of data in a regulatory submission, not to the act of testing. Chemicals with non-cosmetic uses fall outside it.

jurisdictions.name: New Zealand
jurisdictions.headline: A statutory prohibition on animal testing for cosmetics since 2015.

timeline.event: Prohibition on the use of animals in research, testing, or teaching for the purpose of developing a cosmetic.

caveats: There is no accompanying import or marketing ban, so animal-tested cosmetics manufactured elsewhere may still be sold.

jurisdictions.name: Canada
jurisdictions.headline: Testing and reliance on new animal data both prohibited since December 2023.
jurisdictions.instrument: Food and Drugs Act, as amended by Bill C-47 (Budget Implementation Act, 2023, No. 1)

timeline.event: Prohibition takes effect on cosmetic animal testing in Canada, on selling cosmetics that rely on new animal test data to establish safety, and on false ‘cruelty-free’ claims.

jurisdictions.name: Mexico
jurisdictions.headline: The first country in North America to prohibit cosmetic animal testing.
jurisdictions.instrument: Reform to the General Health Law (Ley General de Salud), Article 275 Bis

timeline.event: Reform published in the Diario Oficial de la Federación.
Prohibition fully in force following the two-year transition period.

jurisdictions.name: Colombia
jurisdictions.headline: A testing, manufacturing, and import ban legislated in 2020.

timeline.event: Law 2047 enacted.
Prohibition takes full effect after the four-year transition period.

jurisdictions.name: Brazil
jurisdictions.headline: A federal restriction tied to the availability of validated alternatives, layered over earlier state bans.
jurisdictions.instrument: CONCEA Normative Resolution No. 58 of 2023; various state laws

timeline.event: São Paulo state bans animal testing for cosmetics, the first of several states to do so.
CONCEA Normative Resolution No. 58 prohibits animal testing for cosmetics, perfumes, and personal hygiene products where a validated alternative method exists.

caveats: The prohibition is conditional on the existence of a recognised alternative for the endpoint in question, so its coverage widens as methods are validated rather than all at once.

jurisdictions.name: Türkiye
jurisdictions.headline: Aligned with the EU cosmetics regime.
jurisdictions.instrument: Cosmetics Regulation, harmonised with Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009

timeline.event: Testing and marketing prohibitions mirroring the EU regime take effect.

jurisdictions.name: Switzerland
jurisdictions.headline: Testing prohibited under animal welfare law; the marketing position tracks the EU closely.
jurisdictions.instrument: Animal Welfare Act (TSchG) and Animal Welfare Ordinance

timeline.event: Authorisation for animal testing of cosmetics is not granted, absent an overriding justification that in practice is not met for cosmetic purposes.

caveats: Switzerland is not in the EEA, so EU marketing-ban provisions do not apply automatically; product law is nonetheless closely harmonised.

jurisdictions.name: Guatemala
jurisdictions.headline: An early Latin American prohibition.
jurisdictions.instrument: Decreto 5-2017, Ley de Protección y Bienestar Animal

timeline.event: Animal testing for cosmetics prohibited.
